# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia, and its incidence and prevalence are rising globally [1]. Thromboembolism arising predominantly from the left atrial appendage (LAA) is responsible for most AF-related strokes; in a foundational pathological review, the thrombus was localized to the left atrial appendage in 43% of patients with rheumatic heart disease and in 91% of patients with nonrheumatic atrial fibrillation [2]. This anatomical observation provided the conceptual basis for mechanical LAA exclusion as an alternative to systemic anticoagulation. The LAA is the most common site of thrombosis in AF and can be excluded surgically at the time of cardiac surgery, and percutaneous transcatheter devices were subsequently developed to achieve the same goal less invasively [3].

Although oral anticoagulation with vitamin K antagonists and, more recently, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) effectively reduces stroke, these agents are limited by bleeding risk and underutilization [4]. Percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) emerged to address this gap, particularly in patients at high bleeding risk or with anticoagulation contraindications.

## Pivotal randomized trials

The PROTECT AF trial established proof of concept. Patients (n=707) with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and at least 1 risk factor were randomized to either the Watchman device or continued warfarin in a 2:1 ratio; after device implantation, warfarin was continued for ≈45 days, followed by clopidogrel for 4.5 months and lifelong aspirin [5]. After 2.3±1.1 years of follow-up, the event rates of the composite primary efficacy end point of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death were 3.0% and 4.3% per 100 patient-years in the Watchman and warfarin groups, respectively, which met the criteria for noninferiority [6]. However, an early periprocedural safety hazard, principally pericardial effusion, was identified [7].

The confirmatory PREVAIL trial enrolled higher-risk patients and incorporated new operators [8]. At 18 months, the rate of the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve the prespecified criteria for noninferiority, attributed to an unexpectedly low event rate in the warfarin arm, although early safety events occurred in 2.2% of the Watchman arm, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF [9]. The final PROTECT AF analysis at 3.8 years confirmed durable benefit [10], and a patient-level meta-analysis of both randomized trials demonstrated that LAAC offered stroke prevention comparable to warfarin [11]. The 5-year pooled outcomes from PREVAIL and PROTECT AF showed that LAAC with Watchman provides stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation comparable to warfarin, with additional reductions in major bleeding, particularly hemorrhagic stroke [12]. A pooled net-clinical-benefit analysis further quantified these tradeoffs [13].

## Patients ineligible for anticoagulation and real-world registries

The ASAP study extended LAAC to patients unable to take warfarin. LAA closure with the Watchman device can be safely performed without a warfarin transition, and is a reasonable alternative to consider for patients at high risk for stroke but with contraindications to systemic oral anticoagulation [14]. The large EWOLUTION registry confirmed real-world feasibility: left atrial appendage closure with the Watchman device has a high success rate in complete LAAC with low peri-procedural risk, even in a population with a higher risk of stroke and bleeding, and multiple co-morbidities [15]. Despite the majority of cases being performed by operators with less than 2 years' experience, the procedure was successful in 98.5% [16].

## Comparison with DOACs

The PRAGUE-17 trial was the first randomized comparison of LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients. PRAGUE-17 was a randomized noninferiority trial comparing percutaneous LAAC with DOACs (95% apixaban) in patients with nonvalvular AF and a history of cardioembolism, clinically-relevant bleeding, or both CHA2DS2-VASc ≥3 and HASBLED ≥2 [17]. In long-term follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC [18]. A dedicated bleeding subanalysis reinforced reduced long-term bleeding with the device strategy [19].

## Newer devices and post-ablation use

Next-generation devices have improved sealing and safety. In the PINNACLE FLX trial, the secondary end point of 2-year stroke or systemic embolism was met at 3.4%, and the next-generation Watchman FLX device demonstrated favorable safety and efficacy outcomes [20], with primary outcomes also favorable [21]. The Amulet IDE trial, the largest head-to-head comparison, found that the Amulet occluder was noninferior for safety and effectiveness of stroke prevention compared with the Watchman device and superior for LAA occlusion, although procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet occluder [22]. The SWISS-APERO trial provided additional comparative imaging data [23], and 3-year Amulet IDE outcomes showed comparable clinical endpoints between devices [24].

The OPTION trial addressed LAAC after AF ablation. LAAO was noninferior to OAC for the composite primary endpoint of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolization and was superior to OAC for non–procedure-related bleeding, supporting it as an alternative after ablation [25]; the full report appeared in NEJM [26].

## Complications and device-related thrombus

Device-related thrombus (DRT) remains an important concern. In a pooled analysis, of 1739 patients who received an implant, DRT was seen in 65 patients (3.74%), and DRT was associated with higher rates of stroke and systemic embolism [27]. Predictors and management have been further characterized in registry data [28].

## Guidelines

Reflecting accumulating evidence, the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS guideline upgraded LAAC recommendations [29]: in patients with CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 and a contraindication to long-term OAC, percutaneous LAAO is reasonable (Class 2a), and in patients with moderate to high stroke risk and high bleeding risk on OAC, it may be a reasonable alternative (Class 2b) [30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC has matured from an experimental concept into an evidence-based therapy supported by multiple randomized trials, large registries, and improving device technology. It is now established for stroke prevention in AF patients with contraindications to or high bleeding risk on anticoagulation, with ongoing trials clarifying its role versus contemporary DOAC therapy.
